article.title: Taliban destroys 650 musical Instruments citing music ban
paras: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

The Taliban in Afghanistan's eastern Khost province have destroyed 650 musical instruments and music-related items confiscated during a months-long crackdown on musical instruments, highlighting the continued enforcement of the group's nationwide ban on music.

According to a statement posted on X by Mustaghfir Gurbaz, who identifies himself as a Taliban spokesperson in Khost, officials from the Department for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice burned the items that were seized during operations across the province.

Since returning to power in August 2021, the Taliban have prohibited most forms of music, allowing only certain types of religious vocal chanting. The ban is enforced by the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice.

"Music is forbidden in Islam," ministry spokesman Saif ul Islam Khyber told the Associated Press, arguing that it promotes immoral behavior and distracts people from religious obligations, though many Islamic scholars disagree.

The restrictions have dramatically altered Afghanistan's cultural landscape. Once vibrant music districts, including Kabul's historic Kucha-e-Kharabat neighborhood, have seen music shops replaced by grocery stores, clothing vendors, and household goods businesses.
Many musicians fled Afghanistan following the Taliban takeover, while others hid or smuggled instruments abroad to prevent them from being confiscated or destroyed.

The destruction is Khost is not the first large-scale Taliban campaign against music. In 2024, the group's morality authorities reported seizing and destroying more than 21,000 musical instruments nationwide, an action widely condemned by cultural organizations and musicians as a major blow to Afghanistan's artistic and cultural heritage.
In 2024, Dr. Ahmad Sarmast, founder and director of the Afghanistan National Institute of Music (ANIM), described the campaign as an attack on the country's cultural identity.

"The Taliban's actions are not only an attack on musical instruments, but an assault on the spirit of freedom, creativity, and the vibrant cultural legacy of Afghanistan,” Sarmast said in a statement two years ago. “They have tried to silence the voice of a nation, but music cannot be erased from the hearts and minds of the Afghan people."
ANIM, which relocated from Kabul to Lisbon after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021, continues to support displaced Afghan musicians and preserve the country's musical traditions.
Despite the ban, some Afghan musicians continue to practice their craft secretly.
In a recent Associated Press report, one rubab player speaking anonymously said he continues to play in secret.

"As long as I am alive, I will continue to play," he said. "Perhaps I will do so in secret, but I will not allow the rubab to be silent." The lute-like instrument is widely regarded as Afghanistan's national instrument.

The musician said the ban has devastated his livelihood. Before the Taliban takeover, he taught music and operated a traditional instrument shop. Today, he works as a day laborer and earns only a fraction of his former income.
He also expressed concern that Afghanistan's centuries-old musical traditions risk disappearing if younger generations are unable to learn and perform.
For many Afghan musicians, music represents more than entertainment. It is a family tradition passed from one generation to the next.
The anonymous rubab player said he learned from his father and intends to teach his eldest son despite the risks, viewing music as an essential part of Afghanistan's cultural identity.

Observers say the destruction of musical instruments by the Taliban highlights the tension between the group's religious policies and efforts by many Afghans to preserve the country's artistic and cultural heritage.

As authorities continue enforcing the music ban, musicians across Afghanistan face a difficult choice: abandon their profession, leave the country, or continue practicing in secret while risking arrest and punishment.
zh: 塔利班以「禁止音樂」為由，摧毀了650件樂器
編者註：本文翻譯自美國之音（VOA）達里語原文報導。
阿富汗東部霍斯特省的塔利班組織，已銷毀在為期數月的樂器查緝行動中沒收的650件樂器及與音樂相關的物品，這凸顯該組織持續在全國範圍內執行音樂禁令。
根據自稱是霍斯特省塔利班發言人的穆斯塔格菲爾·古爾巴茲在X平台發布的聲明，宣揚美德與防止邪惡部門的官員焚毀了在該省各地行動中查獲的物品。
自2021年8月重新掌權以來，塔利班已禁止大多數形式的音樂，僅允許特定類型的宗教誦經。這項禁令由「宣揚美德與防止邪惡部」負責執行。
該部發言人賽義夫·烏爾·伊斯蘭·開伯爾（Saif ul Islam Khyber）向美聯社表示：「伊斯蘭教禁止音樂」，並辯稱音樂會助長不道德行為，並使人們疏於履行宗教義務，儘管許多伊斯蘭學者對此持不同意見。
這些限制措施已大幅改變了阿富汗的文化面貌。曾經生機勃勃的音樂區——包括喀布爾歷史悠久的庫查-埃-哈拉巴特（Kucha-e-Kharabat）街區——如今音樂商店已被雜貨店、服裝攤販和家居用品店所取代。
塔利班接管阿富汗後，許多音樂家紛紛逃離該國，而其他人則將樂器藏起來或偷運出境，以避免樂器被沒收或毀壞。
霍斯特的這起破壞事件並非塔利班首次針對音樂發動的大規模行動。2024年，該組織的道德監管機構報告稱，已在全國範圍內查扣並銷毀超過21,000件樂器，此舉遭到文化組織和音樂人的廣泛譴責，被視為對阿富汗藝術與文化遺產的重大打擊。
2024年，阿富汗國家音樂學院（ANIM）創辦人兼院長阿赫邁德·薩爾馬斯特博士將這項運動描述為對該國文化認同的攻擊。
「塔利班的行徑不僅是對樂器的攻擊，更是對自由精神、創造力以及阿富汗蓬勃文化遺產的侵犯，」薩爾馬斯特兩年前在一份聲明中表示。 「他們試圖扼殺一個民族的聲音，但音樂絕不會從阿富汗人民的心中與腦海中被抹去。」
ANIM 組織在 2021 年塔利班於阿富汗重掌大權後，從喀布爾遷至里斯本，至今仍持續支援流離失所的阿富汗音樂家，並致力於保存該國的音樂傳統。
儘管有這項禁令，一些阿富汗音樂家仍繼續秘密地從事他們的音樂創作。
在美聯社最近的一篇報導中，一位不願透露姓名的魯巴布演奏者表示，他至今仍持續在暗中演奏。
「只要我還活著，我就會繼續演奏，」他說。「或許我會偷偷地演奏，但我絕不會讓魯巴布琴沉默。」這種類似魯特琴的樂器，被廣泛視為阿富汗的國樂。
這位音樂家表示，這項禁令徹底摧毀了他的生計。在塔利班接管之前，他曾教授音樂並經營一家傳統樂器店。如今，他靠打零工維生，收入僅有過去的一小部分。
他還表示擔憂，如果年輕一代無法學習和表演，阿富汗流傳數百年的音樂傳統恐將面臨消失的風險。
對許多阿富汗音樂家而言，音樂不僅僅是娛樂。它是代代相傳的家族傳統。
這位不願透露姓名的魯巴布琴演奏者表示，他是跟隨父親學習的，儘管存在風險，他仍打算將這門技藝傳授給長子，因為他認為音樂是阿富汗文化認同不可或缺的一部分。
觀察家指出，塔利班破壞樂器的行為，凸顯了該組織的宗教政策與許多阿富汗人致力於保存該國藝術與文化遺產的努力之間的矛盾。
隨著當局持續執行音樂禁令，阿富汗各地的音樂人面臨艱難的抉擇：放棄職業、離開國門，或是冒著被逮捕和懲處的風險，繼續秘密進行音樂活動。
